control_ladder.note_beginner: Pawpaw growers are told to leave this one alone. A tree opens far more flowers than the borer spoils, and no spray is recommended against it. Cleaning up under the tree is not the answer either, because the caterpillar does not grow up on the ground: it leaves the flower for the stem and twig, turns into a pupa there, and the moths come out of the twigs in spring, often right when the tree is in bloom.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The Kentucky State pawpaw program's advice is that the abundance of unaffected flowers usually does not require controlling this insect, and no product is recommended for it; a small-farm guide calls the damage too slight to be a serious problem. Sanitation has no documented target here. The larvae feed from the anthers through the floral tissue and bore into the stem, pupate in the twigs and emerge from them, with pupal cases visible on the twigs at bloom, so the ground under the tree is not where the cycle completes. A commercial guide recommends orchard sanitation against several other pawpaw insects; that advice is not given for this borer, whose cycle runs from the flower into the stem and twig.

symptoms_seasoned.new: Open flowers wither and drop just as they should be setting fruit. The larva, about 5 millimeters long, feeds unseen inside the fleshy flower tissue and the flower stalk and then bores on into the stem, so the first sign is usually the drop itself. At bloom in spring the adults, small brown moths about a quarter inch long with darker wing tips, emerge from the twigs, and their pupal cases can be seen on the twigs then. In some years the borer destroys the majority of a tree's blossoms, so a heavy bloom yields almost no fruit; in most years the loss is too small to count as a serious problem.
symptoms_seasoned.why: 'blacken' and 'small pale caterpillar' have no anchor: the sources say wither and drop, and no document gives the larva's color. The spring sign the documents do give, moths and pupal cases on the twigs at bloom, was missing, and the year-to-year swing was stated without its usual case.

symptoms_beginner.new: Flowers wither and drop right when they should be turning into fruit. The caterpillar is tiny, about 5 millimeters, and feeds hidden inside the flower and its stalk before boring on into the twig, so you rarely see it. Around bloom in spring you may notice the small brown moths coming out of the twigs, or their pupal cases left on the twigs. In a bad year it can ruin most of the flowers, so a tree that bloomed heavily still gives very few pawpaws; most years the loss is small.
symptoms_beginner.why: Same as symptoms_seasoned: 'turn black' and 'tiny pale caterpillar' are unanchored, and the twig sign at bloom was missing.

organic_treatment_seasoned.new: No product is recommended against this borer, and the pawpaw program's own advice is that the great abundance of unaffected flowers usually does not require controlling it; a small-farm guide rates the damage too slight to be a serious problem. Gathering dropped flowers is no part of that advice, and the life cycle shows why: the larvae leave the floral tissue, bore into the stem, pupate in the twigs and emerge from them, so the flowers on the ground are not where the insect completes its development. The practical response is to accept the year's loss and let the flowers the borer misses carry the crop.
organic_treatment_seasoned.why: The record's flower-sanitation prescription ('gather and destroy dropped, infested flowers to reduce the local population') has no anchor and is contradicted by the life cycle: larvae bore from the flower into the stem and pupate and emerge in the twigs. 'lean on hand pollination... to secure a crop despite the losses' is an inference no document makes, and 'rarely fatal to the tree and often eases the following year' is unsourced.

organic_treatment_beginner.new: There is nothing to spray, and pawpaw growers are told not to try: the tree opens far more flowers than the borer ruins, so it usually does not need controlling. Picking up the fallen flowers is not a fix any pawpaw guide recommends either, because the caterpillar bores on into the twig, where it turns into a moth. Let the flowers it missed make your crop.
organic_treatment_beginner.why: Same as organic_treatment_seasoned: the pick-up-fallen-flowers prescription is off-target for a larva that pupates in the twig, the hand-pollination link is an inference, and 'usually less of a problem the next year' is unsourced.

prevention_seasoned.new: There is no preventive step. The borer completes its cycle inside the stem and twig rather than in litter on the ground, no resistant cultivar is named, and no product is recommended against it. What a grower can do is recognize the year: the small brown moths and their pupal cases on the twigs at bloom signal an active population, and the loss swings from negligible in most years to the majority of blossoms in a bad one. Hand pollination with a small brush is worth doing on pawpaw for fruit set in its own right, since the tree is self-incompatible and usually needs pollen from a genetically different tree, but it is a pollination measure, not a borer control.
prevention_seasoned.why: 'Keep the ground under the tree clear of fallen flowers and debris where the borer can complete its cycle' is wrong: the cycle completes in the stem and twig. Hand pollination as 'pollination insurance' against the borer is an inference; the documents recommend it for fruit set generally.

prevention_beginner.new: You cannot prevent it. The borer lives out its cycle inside the twigs, not in fallen flowers, so raking under the tree does nothing, and no spray or variety is recommended against it. Watch the twigs at bloom for small brown moths and their pupal cases if you want to know whether it is around. Hand pollinating with a small brush is still worth doing on pawpaw, because the tree needs pollen from a different tree to set fruit at all, but that is about pollination, not the borer.
prevention_beginner.why: Same as prevention_seasoned: 'Rake up and remove fallen flowers so the borer cannot keep its cycle going under the tree' is contradicted by the twig life cycle, and hand pollination is recast as the fruit-set measure the documents describe.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Leave them alone if you can. These are the caterpillars of the zebra swallowtail, a butterfly whose young can grow up on no other plant, and on an established tree they chew a few young leaves without coming in numbers that do it any real harm; pawpaw growers are told the feeding is not worth treating. A tree planted this year, or a seedling, is the one exception, because there the caterpillars can eat a large share of the leaves it has. If a small tree is losing more new leaves than you can spare, look over the young growth at the branch tips and lift the caterpillars off by hand. No spray is called for.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Tolerance is the documented answer. The larvae feed only on young pawpaw foliage, on an established tree never in great numbers, they do not affect fruit yield, and the extension advice for a home tree is that the damage does not warrant treatment. The exception is a newly planted tree or seedling, where the larvae can devour much of the foliage: where such a tree is losing new growth faster than it can spare, hand removal is the one intervention that stays selective, and the search is short because the feeding is confined to the new foliage. Anything beyond that removes the larvae of a native butterfly that has no other host, for damage the pawpaw program rates negligible.

symptoms_seasoned.new: Chewed young leaves, usually only a few at a time, with the caterpillars feeding on the new foliage: a green or black caterpillar up to 2 inches long, ringed with narrow green, white, blue or yellow bands, widest at the head and tapering along the body. On a mature tree the damage is light: the larvae do not come in numbers large enough to defoliate it, they do not affect fruit yield, and the feeding rarely amounts to much. A newly planted tree or seedling is the exception: there the larvae can devour much of the foliage.
symptoms_seasoned.why: 'a green-and-black banded caterpillar' was imprecise: the larva is green or black with narrow green, white, blue or yellow bands, so the description is rewritten from the two documents that give it rather than dropped. 'the larvae never appear in numbers large enough to defoliate a tree' is wrong for young trees: a newly planted tree or seedling can lose much of its foliage, so the 'never' is scoped to a mature tree. The rest holds and is kept, with the documents' fruit-yield statement added.

symptoms_beginner.new: A few young leaves chewed here and there at the tips of the branches, with a caterpillar on the new growth: green or black, up to 2 inches long, with thin green, white, blue or yellow rings around its body, and widest at the head end. On an established tree the damage is minor: there are never enough of them to strip it, and they do not cost you any fruit. A tree you planted this year, or a seedling, can lose a lot of its leaves to them.

cause_seasoned.new: Larvae of the zebra swallowtail butterfly (Protographium marcellus, also listed as Eurytides marcellus), for which pawpaw is the sole larval host plant. The caterpillars feed only on young pawpaw foliage and never in great numbers, so they are far more a delight than a threat: the striking adult butterfly depends entirely on pawpaw.

control_ladder.note_beginner: You will not out-wait a raccoon, so pick first. Pawpaws are ready when the flesh just starts to soften and the skin gives a little under your thumb; pick them then and let them finish ripening on the counter, because fruit picked while it is still firm will not ripen. Go by feel, not color: a ripe pawpaw can still be green. Once ripening starts, in late summer and early fall, check the tree every day, and pick up anything that has dropped, since deer and every other animal will clean up fallen fruit.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Harvest timing carries the home defense. Pick at the first give of the flesh, when the skin indents slightly to a finger squeeze, and finish ripening off the tree; fruit taken slightly under-ripe ripens, fruit taken firm does not, and a color change is not a reliable signal, so the window is narrow and worth walking daily. Ripening runs from August into October, and drops need clearing, because the ground under the tree is where deer join the raccoons, opossums, squirrels and foxes.

symptoms_seasoned.new: Ripe and nearly ripe fruit disappears from the tree or is found half-eaten on the ground, right as it softens. Ripe pawpaw is prized by wildlife and quickly eaten, and the harvest window is short, so the animals frequently take the fruit before the gardener does.
symptoms_seasoned.why: 'often overnight' and 'soft fruit is highly aromatic' as the reason animals come have no anchor: no document times the raids or ties them to the fruit's smell. The rest holds.
symptoms_seasoned.anchor: uiuc_ext 'The ripe fruit is prized by wildlife and quickly eaten.' / 'To successfully harvest the fruit, diligence is necessary.'

symptoms_beginner.new: Ripe or almost-ripe fruit vanishes from the tree or turns up chewed on the ground, just as it gets soft. Wild animals prize ripe pawpaws and eat them fast, so they often get to the fruit before you do.
symptoms_beginner.why: Same as symptoms_seasoned: 'usually overnight' and 'The strong ripe smell draws animals' are unanchored.
symptoms_beginner.anchor: uiuc_ext 'The ripe fruit is prized by wildlife and quickly eaten.'

cause_seasoned.new: Raccoons, opossums, squirrels, and foxes all eat pawpaw fruit, ripe on the tree or fallen beneath it, through the August-to-October ripening season. Deer avoid the foliage and twigs, which chemicals in the bark and leaves make unpalatable, but they do eat ripe fruit that has dropped, so they belong here as scavengers of fallen fruit rather than as browsers. The other deer damage is physical: bucks rub their antlers on trunks in winter and can seriously injure the bark of an unprotected tree.
cause_seasoned.why: 'Deer, by contrast, avoid the foliage and fruit' is wrong on the fruit half: the pawpaw program, Clemson and ACES all say deer eat dropped or ripe fruit. Foxes, named in every document that names the other three, were missing, and so was the antler-rub damage the documents describe. The 'attracted to the intense aroma' link is an inference and is dropped.

Male deer occasionally damage trees by rubbing their antlers on them in winter.'; clemson_hgic 'Foxes, feral pigs, opossums, and raccoons eat the fruit. organic_treatment_seasoned.new: Beat the animals to the fruit. Pick pawpaws as the flesh first starts to soften, when the skin gives slightly under a finger, and finish ripening them indoors; fruit picked slightly under-ripe ripens off the tree, fruit picked firm does not. Check the tree daily through the ripening period and do not leave dropped fruit on the ground, where deer join the rest. Prompt picking is the practical defense for a home tree.
organic_treatment_seasoned.why: 'Netting or trunk baffles help where pressure is heavy' has no anchor; no document mentions either for pawpaw. The harvest guidance holds and is kept, tightened to the documents' ripeness signal (skin gives slightly; never firm).

organic_treatment_beginner.new: Get to the fruit first. Pick pawpaws as soon as the flesh starts to soften and the skin gives a little when you press it, then let them finish ripening indoors. Do not pick them while they are still firm, because they will not ripen, and do not wait for the skin to change color, because a ripe pawpaw can still be green. Check the tree every day while it is ripening, and pick up any fruit that has dropped so it does not feed the deer and everything else. Picking on time is the defense.
organic_treatment_beginner.why: Same as organic_treatment_seasoned: 'Netting or a baffle on the trunk can help' is unanchored; the pick-firm risk the documents warn about is stated, and it is stated as firmness rather than color, because a pawpaw is green- or yellow-skinned when ripe and color change is not a ripeness cue.

control_ladder.note_beginner: This fungus needs the leaves and fruit to stay wet for a long stretch, from rain or heavy dew, and it is worst in humid places and rainy summers. Plant the tree where air moves, leave it room, and prune out crowded growth so the canopy dries quickly after a wet night. Nothing in a bottle backs this up, because no fungicide is labeled for pawpaw.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Prolonged wetness of foliage and fruit is the infection condition, so leaf-wetness duration is the lever: site and space for air movement and prune to open dense foliage, the measures a small-farm guide credits with reducing it. It prevents rather than rescues, so it is a planting decision and a routine, and it matters most in the wet years when the fruit spots merge and the fruit cracks. It carries the load because no fungicide is labeled for the crop.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Rake up the fallen leaves from under a spotted tree as they drop and get rid of them, never into the compost pile: the spots keep shedding spores onto healthy leaves in wet weather. If only a few leaves are spotted you can just pick those off, cleaning your hands and tools before you touch another plant. A fruit that has cracked will quickly rot, so do not count on it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The spotted tissue carries the fungus's fruiting bodies, which release spores onto healthy foliage in wet weather, so leaf litter under an infected tree is the reservoir to strip: remove it as the leaves fall and do not compost it. A light infestation can be handled by picking off the spotted leaves, sterilizing tools and hands between passes. Cracked fruit is colonized by other organisms and insects almost at once and is a loss, not a fruit to salvage.

symptoms_seasoned.new: Tan spots with brown borders on the leaves that darken to brown or black lesions, and hard black spots on the fruit skin. Spotting alone seldom has any effect on flavor or edibility. In a wet year, though, the fruit spots merge and the fruit cracks as it develops; once the flesh is exposed it is quickly colonized by other rots and by insects, and that fruit is lost. Leaves are affected too, but the tree is not killed. Infection needs leaves or fruit to stay wet from rain or dew for a prolonged period, so humid climates and wet years are where it bites. Flyspeck is a different and purely cosmetic fungus that also marks the fruit surface without affecting edibility; the difference is that this one merges, cracks the fruit and opens it to rot.
symptoms_seasoned.why: 'The spotting is cosmetic: it does not defoliate a healthy tree or spoil the flesh, and the fruit inside remains sound' is wrong for Phyllosticta: Clemson calls it a severe disease that cracks the fruit, MU says the cracked flesh is quickly infected, KSU PBI-004 says infested fruit splits. The surface-only, still-edible description fits flyspeck, which the record had fused into this entry, and it fits this fungus only for fruit that has not cracked: the pawpaw program says hard black patches alone seldom affect flavor or edibility, and that sentence is kept so the correction does not swing from 'cosmetic' to 'ruined'.

This disease causes hard black spots to form on the fruit skin, which often merge and leads to premature cracking. Leaves are affected too, but the tree is not killed.' / 'A cosmetic fungal disease known as flyspeck (Zygophiala jamaicensis), has been reported on pawpaw. However, the fungus only grows on the surface of the fruit and does not prevent it from being edible.'; mu_ext 'Symptoms of this disease first appear as tan spots with brown borders, but later form dark brown to black lesions. Symptoms are similar on the fruit, but lesions can eventually crack open. When the flesh is exposed from cracking, it quickly becomes infected with other disease organisms and insects, resulting in unmarketable fruit.' / 'When foliage or fruit remains wet from rainfall or dew for a prolonged period of time, infection can occur.'; ksu_pawpaw (PBI-004) 'Especially during wet years, fungal spot (Phyllosticta species) on leaves and the surface of fruit can lead to problems; infested fruit can to split during development.'; ksu_pawpaw (Pawpaw Planting Guide, https://www.kysu.edu/academics/college-ahnr/school-of-anr/pawpaw/pawpaw-planting-guide.php) 'Sometimes the fruit surface may be covered with patches that are hard and black; this is a fungus infection, but it seldom has any effect on flavor or edibility.'

symptoms_beginner.new: Small tan spots with brown edges on the leaves that turn dark, and hard black spots on the fruit skin. Spots on their own seldom change how the fruit tastes or whether you can eat it. In a wet year, though, the fruit spots run together and the fruit splits open as it grows; the split lets rot and insects in, and that fruit is ruined. The leaves get spotted too, but the tree itself is not killed. It shows up most in humid places and wet summers, because the fungus needs the leaves and fruit to stay wet for a long stretch.
symptoms_beginner.why: Same as symptoms_seasoned: 'It looks worse than it is: the spots are just on the surface... and the fruit inside is fine' is refuted for cracked fruit by every document that names the fungus; the pawpaw program's reassurance for merely spotted fruit is kept.

organic_treatment_seasoned.new: No fungicide is labeled for pawpaw, so a spray is not an option whatever a product might do on other fruit. Management is cultural: spacing and pruning for ventilation, since dense foliage and still air keep leaves and fruit wet, and removal of the fallen leaves from under an infected tree as they drop, without composting them. Where only a few leaves are spotted, picking them off is enough, with tools and hands sterilized between passes. Fruit that has cracked is quickly invaded by other rots and insects and will not keep.
organic_treatment_seasoned.why: 'No fungicide is warranted for what is a cosmetic issue' gives the wrong reason: the disease cracks fruit, and the reason no fungicide is used is that none is labeled for pawpaw. 'keep the tree vigorous' has no anchor, and 'The fruit is unaffected inside and fully edible' is refuted.

Fruit that has cracked will quickly rot.

prevention_seasoned.new: Space and site trees for air movement and prune to open a dense canopy, so foliage and fruit dry quickly after rain and dew. Clear the fallen leaves as they drop and keep them out of the compost. Wet years and humid climates are when it does damage. Susceptibility appears to vary among varieties, but nothing comprehensive has been published, so no cultivar can be recommended for resistance.

prevention_beginner.new: Give trees enough space for air to move and prune out crowded growth so the leaves dry fast after rain. Rake up and remove the fallen leaves as they drop, and keep them out of the compost. Wet, muggy summers are when it does damage. No variety is known to resist it yet.

ACES SCOPE FINDING: the brief describes ACES's 'Trapping, manual removal, and orchard cleanliness and sanitation' sentence as spanning its whole list. Read in context it is the closing sentence of the 'Other pawpaw pests may include...' paragraph (stinging rose caterpillar, sphinx moth, granulate ambrosia beetle, BMSB, SWD); the peduncle borer has its own earlier section with no control statement. That is why the borer ladder is a refusal rather than a scoped sanitation rung.

ONE-URL-PER-KEY: ksu_pawpaw has four relevant documents on this crop. The borer entry anchors the planting guide (binomial, 5 mm, 'majority of blossoms', self-incompatibility; it closes the cert finding on the existing anchor); the Phyllosticta entry anchors PBI-004 per the brief. The borer's load-bearing 'does not require control' sentence is in PBI-004 and is quoted with its URL inside the correction anchors. umd_ext likewise: the wildlife entry anchors Native Trees (the four animals, August-October); the antler-rub and never-pick-firm sentences are on Less Common Fruits and are quoted with that URL inside the correction anchors.

ncsu_ext SCOPE: the Phyllosticta entry anchors a county article at lee.ces.ncsu.edu (NC State Extension, Lee County; Bratcher 2023, updated 2025-07-31), same *.ces.ncsu.edu family as the toolbox and written from a pawpaw case. It is the only admissible document prescribing leaf-litter removal, no composting, and pick-off-plus-sterilize. Flagging in case the key's scope is read as content.ces.ncsu.edu only.

cornell_small_farms is used on the borer and Phyllosticta entries. It is a T1 catalog key (extension_program, 'particularly strong for specialty crop and small-scale production guidance'), it was an ANCHORS line in the record report, and I re-read it first-party today. It carries the only spacing-and-pruning prescription for this leaf spot and the 'not considered a serious problem' framing for the borer.
